newsitem.title: USA: Miami chilled by prospect of American strike.
newsitem.headline: Miami chilled by prospect of American strike.

text.p: The prospect of a pilot's strike this month at AMR Corp.'s American Airlines has sent a chill through Miami's balmy February, leaving community leaders pleading with the two sides to settle their differences without a walkout.

Though the airline is based in Dallas, it is an integral player in Miami's economy, particularly its identity as a centre for Latin American trade and tourism. And the threat of a strike on Feb. 15 could hardly come at a worse time for the city, the height of the winter tourist season and a time when Miami is wrestling with a $68 million budget deficit.

"The citizens of Dade County have been watching with growing concern the labour dispute and possible strike between the pilots and American Airlines management," said a full-page advertisement taken out in the Miami Herald on Wednesday by the Beacon Council, Coalition of Chambers of Commerce and Greater Miami Convention & Visitors Bureau.
"This labour dispute goes far beyond pilots and management," the business groups said, noting the economic importance of the airline to Miami and calling on the two sides to resume negotiations.
The ad also called on private citizens to write or send electronic mail to the White House, asking President Clinton to step in to avoid the strike.

American is the largest air cargo carrier through Miami International Airport, hauling 148,935 tons during the first nine months of last year. And with 95 percent of visitors to Miami arriving by air, the airline accounts for just over half of total airline seats, or about 300,000 passengers a month and 200 flights a day.
Travellers already have been scrambling to schedule trips without the risk of getting stranded by a walkout, and quailed at the prospect of doing business without the carrier.
"Probably 80 percent of the people that fly to Latin America use American," said Santiago Aragon, who runs the Miami-based Latin American division of Expeditors International of Washington Inc.
"We would have to look to other airlines and they are already overbooked. We'd have to make business travel arrangements months in advance," he said.

American has about 9,200 employees in Dade County. According to a study prepared for the airline by National Economic Research Associates last fall, the airline accounts for more than 114,000 jobs in greater Miami, or about 9.8 percent of the area's total employment.

"An American Airlines work stoppage, for South Florida, would have a devastating impact for this entire community," said Frank Nero, president and chief executive officer of the Beacon Council, Dade County's economic development agency.

The prospect of a large-scale strike is especially chilling in Miami, which saw Eastern Airlines, once South Florida's premier airline, shut down in 1991 after a crippling strike and a mountain of debt forced it into bankruptcy.

"It still brings back some chilling memories to the folks in South Florida where they literally watched management and labour unable to come to an agreement and, of course, ultimately the demise of that airline," Nero said.

The carrier and its pilots must reach a contract agreement by 0001 est (0501 GMT) on Feb. 15, the end of a legally mandated cooling off period, and the Allied Pilots Association has promised to launch a strike the minute the walkout is legal.
